# On Wandering Without a Map

I want to write about the experience of not knowing what to write about, because that paradox feels more honest than pretending I arrived here with some burning thesis. There's something instructive in starting from genuine uncertainty rather than performing certainty I don't have. So let me think out loud, in print, about whatever surfaces.

The first thing that comes to mind is the strange nature of attention itself. We talk about "paying" attention, as if it were currency, as if there's a finite account from which we draw and which can be depleted. This metaphor has become so embedded in how we think about focus that we rarely examine it. But what if attention isn't a resource at all, but more like a muscle, or even more strangely, like a doorway? You don't pay a doorway. You walk through it, and what's on the other side either holds you or it doesn't.

I've been thinking about how much of contemporary life is organized around capturing this supposedly scarce resource. Every app, every notification, every headline is engineered by people who have studied, with considerable rigor, the exact mechanisms by which human attention can be hooked and held. There's an entire science to it now—variable reward schedules borrowed from slot machine design, the dopamine hit of a notification badge, the infinite scroll that never lets you reach a natural stopping point because natural stopping points are precisely what the design wants to eliminate. We know this. It's not secret information. And yet knowing it changes remarkably little about our behavior, which suggests that the gap between knowledge and action is wider and stranger than we usually admit.

This makes me think about willpower, another concept I'm suspicious of. We treat willpower as if it's a property of character, a moral fiber that some people have in abundance and others lack, as if resisting the urge to check your phone for the fortieth time in an hour is a referendum on your fundamental worth as a person. But this seems backward. The people who seem to have the most "willpower" are usually just the people who have arranged their environments so that temptation requires more steps to reach. They've made the friction asymmetric. The phone is in another room. The browser has a blocker. The bad food isn't in the house. This isn't moral superiority; it's structural engineering. And yet we persist in talking about self-control as though it were a personal virtue rather than, in large part, a design problem.

I wonder if this same misattribution happens in lots of domains. We see outcomes and we narrate them in terms of character when they might be better explained by circumstance, structure, timing, luck. The successful person becomes a genius; the unsuccessful person becomes lazy or unfocused. But success and failure are so often downstream of conditions that have nothing to do with the inner qualities we attribute them to. This isn't a particularly novel observation, but it's one I keep rediscovering, as if my mind resets its understanding of this every few months and has to relearn it through fresh examples.

Let me pivot, because I notice I'm circling something resembling a moral argument and I'm not sure that's where I want to go. What else is sitting in the back of my mind?

Rivers. I keep thinking about rivers, for no reason I can immediately identify, except that there's something in the structure of a river that feels like a good model for thought itself. A river doesn't go in a straight line. It meanders because the path of least resistance is rarely a straight line; it curves around obstacles, deposits sediment in slower sections, carves deeper in faster ones. Over time, given enough freedom, a river will wander across an entire floodplain, leaving traces of where it used to be in the form of oxbow lakes and old channels that no longer carry water but still hold the shape of the river's history.

Thought seems to work this way too, at least for me, at least right now. I started this piece thinking about attention and willpower, and now I'm thinking about rivers, and the connection between these isn't a straight line of logic but something more like a meander—each thought depositing something, each digression carving slightly into the next idea, until you have a landscape that makes sense only in retrospect, if it makes sense at all.

There's a kind of writing that insists on a thesis from the first sentence, that announces its argument and then marches through evidence in support of that argument. This has its uses. It's the structure of most essays you'd be taught to write in school, the five-paragraph format, the topic sentence followed by support. But it's a fairly unnatural way to think, even if it's a useful way to communicate conclusions once you've already reached them. The actual process of thinking, at least as I experience it, is much closer to the river. You don't know where you're going until you've gone there. The path reveals the destination rather than the destination dictating the path.

This is, I think, why I find writing without a predetermined topic clarifying rather than anxiety-inducing, even though it should probably be the opposite. There's a vulnerability in not knowing what you're going to say, in trusting that something will emerge from the act of putting words down rather than from some prior planning phase. But there's also a freedom in it. The blank page becomes less like an exam question demanding a correct answer and more like an unmapped territory you get to wander through, noticing what's there.

I think about how children seem to operate this way more naturally before they're trained out of it. Watch a child play and you'll notice that their attention moves fluidly, following interest rather than obligation. They don't need a reason to be curious about a beetle on the sidewalk; the beetle is interesting because it's there, because it's moving in a way that's slightly alien and slightly familiar at the same time. The whole apparatus of justification—why does this matter, what's the point, how does this serve some larger goal—comes later, layered on by an education system and a culture that has decided, reasonably enough in some contexts, that not everything can be pursued purely for its own sake, that there are limited hours and resources have to be allocated according to some hierarchy of importance.

But something is lost in this transition, even if something is also gained. The capacity for purposeless attention—attention that doesn't need to justify itself by reference to outcomes—seems to atrophy unless it's deliberately maintained. And maybe this is part of why people seek out hobbies, or meditation, or long walks without destinations: not because these activities are unproductive, exactly, but because they offer a return to a mode of attention that doesn't have to answer to anything outside itself.

I'm aware that I'm now making an argument, somewhat against my own initial impulse to resist argument-making. Maybe that's unavoidable. Maybe even the river, despite its meandering, still has a directionality—it flows downhill, after all, even if the specific path is unpredictable. Maybe thought is similar: it can wander locally while still trending toward something, some accumulation of perspective or insight that emerges not because you forced it but because you let enough material flow through long enough that patterns started to assert themselves.

Let me follow another digression. I think about translation, and how something is always lost when you move between languages, but also how something can be gained. There are words in other languages that don't have direct English equivalents—the German word for the specific kind of joy you feel at someone else's misfortune, the Portuguese word for a particular flavor of longing or nostalgia, the Japanese concept of finding beauty in imperfection or transience. These words exist because some culture, over a long period of time, found it useful or necessary to name a feeling precisely, and the act of naming it made it more visible, more discussable, more real in a social sense.

This makes me wonder what feelings or states exist in my own experience that don't have names yet, that I haven't been given the linguistic tools to identify clearly. There's probably a vast territory of subjective experience that goes unnamed simply because no one has needed to name it precisely enough, or because the names that exist are close enough approximations that we've never bothered to refine further. Language is a net we throw over experience, and the mesh size of that net determines how much detail we can catch.

I think about how this relates to emotional intelligence, or whatever we want to call the capacity to identify and work with one's own internal states. Part of what makes someone skilled in this domain might simply be a richer vocabulary for distinguishing between adjacent feelings—the difference between disappointment and resignation, between anxiety and excitement (which share so much physiological overlap that the distinction is sometimes more interpretive than visceral), between loneliness and solitude. If you only have a few words for emotional states, you're forced to lump together experiences that might actually be quite different, and this lumping might itself cause problems, might prevent you from responding appropriately because you've misidentified what you're dealing with.

This is, I think, part of why writing can be therapeutic, even when it's not explicitly therapeutic writing, even when you're not trying to process trauma or sit with grief. The act of finding words for something vague forces a kind of precision that pure feeling doesn't have. The vague cloud of unease in your chest becomes, through the effort of writing, something more specific: maybe it's dread about a particular conversation you need to have, or maybe it's a more general anxiety about mortality that's been triggered by something small, or maybe it's just hunger, misread by a brain that's bad at distinguishing its signals. You don't know until you try to write it down, until you try to find the word that fits.

I notice now that I've wandered fairly far from where I started, and I'm curious whether there's a way to loop back, the way a river sometimes curves around and almost touches its earlier path, creating those oxbow shapes I mentioned before. Attention, willpower, rivers, childhood curiosity, translation, emotional vocabulary—is there a thread here, or have I simply been listing things that occurred to me in sequence?

Maybe the thread is something about precision and its absence. Attention becomes commodified when we stop being precise about what it actually is and start treating it as a generic resource to be captured. Willpower becomes a moral category when we're imprecise about the actual mechanics of behavior change, when we ignore the role of environment and structure. Rivers find their paths through a kind of precision that isn't conscious—water finding exactly the path of least resistance, which is its own form of precision, just not a deliberative one. Childhood curiosity is precise in its attention to specific things—that beetle, not beetles in general—before it gets flattened into generic categories of what's "supposed" to be interesting. Translation reveals the imprecision of any single language, the way meaning slips between the nets we throw over it. Emotional vocabulary is precision applied to internal states that would otherwise remain undifferentiated blobs of feeling.

Maybe what I'm circling, without quite landing on it, is something about the relationship between precision and freedom. We tend to think of precision as constraining—more rules, more specificity, less room to move. But maybe precision is actually what enables freedom, in the sense that knowing exactly what you're dealing with, having the right words and the right distinctions, gives you more options for how to respond, rather than fewer. The person with a rich emotional vocabulary isn't more constrained by their feelings; they're more able to work with them precisely because they can distinguish between them. The river that has carved a precise channel over time isn't less free than a river that floods chaotically over a wide floodplain with no clear path; it's actually more powerful, more capable of sustained directional flow, precisely because of the constraint it has developed over time.

This reframes something for me. I had been thinking about this essay's lack of a predetermined structure as a kind of freedom—and it has been, in some sense—but maybe the deeper freedom would come not from refusing structure altogether but from finding the structure that the material itself wants, the channel that the thinking actually wants to carve, rather than imposing a structure from outside or refusing structure entirely and calling that freedom. Pure formlessness isn't freedom; it's just a different kind of constraint, the constraint of having no direction at all, which can be just as limiting as having too rigid a direction.

I think this might be why the best writing, the best thinking, often feels both surprising and inevitable at the same time. Surprising because you didn't see it coming, because it wasn't planned from the outset; inevitable because once it arrives, it feels like the only place the thinking could have ended up, given everything that came before. This is the river finding the sea. It wasn't predetermined in the sense of being planned, but it also wasn't random—it was the necessary consequence of terrain, gravity, water, and time all interacting according to their nature.

I don't know if I've arrived anywhere with this piece that constitutes a destination rather than just a place where I happened to stop. Maybe that's fine. Maybe the value isn't in arrival but in the wandering itself, in the texture of thought moving through territory without a map, depositing sediment, carving channels, occasionally surprising itself with where it ends up. I started not knowing what to write about and I find myself, two thousand five hundun words later, having written about attention and rivers and emotional precision and the strange relationship between constraint and freedom, without having planned any of it in advance.

Maybe that's the only honest way to write about not knowing what to write about: to let the not-knowing become its own subject, to trust that wandering, done attentively enough, generates its own kind of meaning—not because you forced it to mean something, but because attention itself, sustained over time, naturally starts to find patterns, connections, oxbow lakes that mark where the thinking used to be before it moved on to somewhere else.
